What makes up the central nervous system (CNS)?
All the nerves in the body
CNS = brain + spinal cord. It is the main control centre that interprets information and decides the response.
The nerves running from the spinal cord to the arms and legs belong to the…
The PNS is all the nerves outside the CNS; it connects the brain and spinal cord to muscles, organs and receptors.

Which of the following is part of the peripheral nervous system?
I. Sensory nerves from the skin
II. The spinal cord
III. Motor nerves to the quadriceps
The spinal cord belongs to the CNS; all nerves outside it (sensory and motor) form the PNS.
According to the syllabus, the efferent division is subdivided into…
Efferent → autonomic (involuntary) + somatic (voluntary). The autonomic then splits into sympathetic and parasympathetic.
The autonomic nervous system is divided into the…
ANS = sympathetic ('fight or flight') + parasympathetic ('rest and digest').
A player rolls their ankle and feels pain. Which type of nerve carries this information TO the CNS?
Afferent = arrives at the CNS (sensory). Trick: Afferent = Arrives, Efferent = Exits.
Carry commands from the CNS to muscles, glands and organs
Carry information from receptors to the brain
Efferent nerves exit the CNS towards the effectors (muscles, glands, organs) to produce a response.
Which type of nerve carries information from muscles and joints to the CNS, helping athletes maintain balance and body awareness?
Sensory (afferent) nerves carry information from receptors such as proprioceptors to the CNS.
A basketball player touches a hot surface and pulls her hand away. Which sequence describes the flow of information?
Receptor → efferent neuron → CNS → afferent neuron → muscle
Receptor → afferent neuron → CNS → efferent neuron → muscle
CNS → afferent neuron → receptor → efferent neuron → muscle
Muscle → efferent neuron → CNS → afferent neuron → receptor
Information is sensed, travels in via afferent neurons, is processed in the CNS, then goes out via efferent neurons to the muscle.
Which of the following is correctly matched?
Autonomic nervous system – controls voluntary skeletal muscle
Somatic nervous system – controls voluntary movement of skeletal muscle
Parasympathetic nervous system – prepares the body for 'fight or flight'
Somatic = voluntary skeletal muscle; autonomic = involuntary functions such as digestion.
You decide to kick a ball. Which system controls this voluntary skeletal muscle movement?
The somatic nervous system controls voluntary movements of skeletal muscles.
Which of these functions is controlled by the AUTONOMIC nervous system?
The ANS regulates involuntary functions: heart rate, digestion, respiration and the stress response.
Link afferent neurons to motoneurons and have an excitatory or inhibitory effect
Interneurons act as a bridge between incoming information and outgoing commands, and can boost or block the signal.

Afferent neurons sense factors such as:
I. Body temperature
II. Blood pressure
III. Blood O₂ and CO₂ levels
Afferent neurons sense body temperature, blood pressure and blood O₂/CO₂ levels.
A sprinter in the blocks waiting for the gun: heart rate rises and breathing speeds up. Which system is active?
The sympathetic system prepares for 'fight or flight': ↑ heart rate, dilated airways, mobilised energy.
After an intense match, heart rate drops and digestion restarts. Which system does this?
Parasympathetic = 'rest and digest': ↓ heart rate, ↑ digestion, promotes recovery.
During a high-intensity workout, which division increases heart rate, blood flow to muscles and energy release?
The sympathetic division increases body activity during stress or exercise.
A cyclist starts climbing a steep hill. Which combination of responses is caused by the sympathetic nervous system?
↑ heart rate, ↑ breathing rate, ↑ blood flow to muscles
↑ heart rate, ↑ digestion, ↓ blood flow to muscles
↓ heart rate, ↑ blood flow to muscles, ↑ digestion
Sympathetic activity raises heart rate, breathing rate and blood flow to working muscles. Digestion is parasympathetic.
INTRINSIC control of heart rate is due to…
The SA node, the heart's pacemaker
Intrinsic = from inside the heart: the SA node generates the rhythm on its own.
Which is an example of EXTRINSIC control of heart rate?
Sympathetic nerves increase it and parasympathetic nerves decrease it
The SA node generates the heartbeat
Extrinsic = factors outside the heart (nerves) that modify the rhythm set by the SA node.
Which statement best describes how intrinsic and extrinsic mechanisms work together to control heart rate?
The SA node sets the rhythm and autonomic nerves speed it up or slow it down
Autonomic nerves set the rhythm and the SA node stops it
The somatic nervous system sets the rhythm
Only the parasympathetic system controls heart rate
Intrinsic (SA node) generates the beat; extrinsic (sympathetic ↑, parasympathetic ↓) modifies the rate.
Which part of the brain adjusts breathing rate according to O₂ and CO₂ levels?
The brain stem regulates basic life functions: breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.

A tennis player competes in 35 °C heat. Which responses are triggered by the hypothalamus?
I. Vasodilation of skin blood vessels
II. Shivering
III. Sweating
To cool down: vasodilation and sweating. Shivering produces heat, so it happens in the cold.
During a swim in cold water, the body keeps warm through…
Vasoconstriction reduces blood flow to the skin (less heat loss) and shivering generates heat.
Why does vasodilation help a runner cool down?
It reduces blood flow to the skin
It sends more warm blood to the skin so heat can be lost
Wider skin vessels bring warm blood near the surface, where heat is lost to the environment.
Which structure detects body temperature changes and triggers sweating or shivering?
The hypothalamus (part of the diencephalon) controls temperature regulation.
During a sprint, blood CO₂ rises and breathing rate increases. Which receptors detect this?
Chemoreceptors detect chemical changes (O₂, CO₂, pH) in the carotid arteries and aorta.
Which receptors help a sprinter's body detect changes in oxygen levels and adjust breathing rate?
Chemoreceptors respond to chemical changes such as O₂ and CO₂ levels.
A rugby player stands up quickly after a scrum and his heart rate adjusts to maintain blood pressure. Which receptors detected the change?
Standing quickly changes blood pressure; baroreceptors (baro = pressure) detect it.
In the aorta and carotid arteries
Proprioceptors report body position and movement, so they sit in muscles, tendons and joints.
Where are chemoreceptors and baroreceptors mainly located?
Both monitor the blood leaving the heart, in the carotid arteries and aorta.
A gymnast keeps her balance on the beam without looking at her feet. Which receptors are key?
Proprioceptors provide information on body position, essential for balance.
Which receptor is correctly matched with what it detects?
Chemoreceptors detect O₂, CO₂ and pH; baroreceptors detect pressure; proprioceptors detect position.
The cerebellum plays an essential role in sport by:
Interpreting sensory information for voluntary muscle control
Managing balance, coordination and fine motor skills
The cerebellum is critical for coordinating movement.
What is the centre of CONSCIOUS motor control (thought, voluntary movement, perception)?
The cerebral cortex is the outer layer of the brain: conscious thought, voluntary movement and perception.
The diencephalon (thalamus and hypothalamus) is mainly responsible for…
Maintaining the internal environment: temperature, hunger, sleep
Connecting the brain to the spinal cord
The diencephalon is a major control centre for the body's internal environment.
Which structure connects the brain to the spinal cord?
The brain stem links brain and spinal cord and controls basic life functions.
What is the correct pathway for a touch on the skin to be consciously perceived?
Skin → peripheral nerve → spinal cord → thalamus → somatosensory cortex
Skin → spinal cord → peripheral nerve → cerebellum → thalamus
Skin → thalamus → spinal cord → peripheral nerve → cortex
Skin → brain stem → cerebellum → spinal cord
The thalamus relays the signal to the somatosensory cortex, which interprets it.
What is the role of the thalamus in sensory processing?
It interprets the type and location of sensation
It acts as a relay centre sending sensory information to the correct brain area
The thalamus relays; the somatosensory cortex interprets.
What is the function of the myelin sheath?
Insulates the electrical signal from surrounding tissues
Releases the signal to the muscle
Myelin insulates the axon; its gaps (nodes of Ranvier) aid transmission.
Which part of the neuron links to other neurons to receive information?
Dendrites link the neuron to other neurons and let information flow between nerves.
Which part of a neuron is the cell body, found in the spinal cord or in ganglia?
The soma is the cell body, located in the spinal cord or in clusters just outside it called ganglia.
At the neuromuscular junction, the end of the axon is:
Unmyelinated, with a small gap (synapse) between neuron and muscle fibre
Directly fused to the muscle fibre
At the motor end plate the axon is unmyelinated and a synapse separates it from the muscle fibre.
A muscle with all its tendons
A single motoneuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates
Motor unit = 1 motoneuron + the fibres it stimulates (10 to 2,000).
The number of neurons in the spinal cord
The number of muscle fibres stimulated by one motoneuron
The speed of a nerve impulse
The ratio of agonists to antagonists
Innervation ratio = muscle fibres per motoneuron.
Eye muscles have very few fibres per motoneuron. What does this achieve?
Few fibres per motoneuron = small forces with fine control. Many fibres (gluteus maximus) = large forces.
When a motoneuron fires, all its fibres contract or none do. This is the…
The fibres of a motor unit are either all relaxed or all contracted.
Given the all-or-nothing principle, how does a muscle produce a stronger contraction?
The antagonist contracts at the same time
Each unit is all-or-nothing, so more force comes from recruiting more motor units.
A marathon runner relies mainly on which motor units?
Type I: small forces, long contractions, fatigue resistant.
A shot putter needs maximum force in one explosive movement. Which motor units matter most?
Type IIa, because they never fatigue
Type IIb: fastest contractions and largest forces, but fatigue quickly.
A 400 m runner needs strong contractions that are fairly fatigue resistant. Which motor units fit best?
Type IIa (fast oxidative): fast, strong and resistant to fatigue.
Which statement about Type I motor units is correct?
Slow transmission, small forces, long contractions, fatigue resistant
Strong forces but fatigue within seconds
Type I = slow twitch: slow, small forces, long lasting, fatigue resistant.
Which functions are mainly provided by the AXIAL skeleton?
Protection of vital organs and support of posture
Attachment points for limb muscles for movement
Forming the shoulder and hip joints
Axial (skull, vertebral column, ribs, sternum) = protection and posture; appendicular = movement.
Haemopoiesis refers to which function of the skeleton?

Which of the following are functions of the skeleton?
I. Storage of calcium and phosphorus
II. Blood cell production
III. Attachment points for muscles
All three are skeletal functions, along with protection, support and energy storage.
How many vertebrae are in the thoracic region?
How many lumbar vertebrae are there?
What is the main advantage of the curves of the vertebral column?
They reduce the number of vertebrae
The curves increase the strength of the vertebral column.
Intervertebral discs (cartilaginous joints) sit between vertebrae.
Which bones form the pectoral (shoulder) girdle?
Pectoral girdle = clavicle + scapula; the humerus joins the scapula at the shoulder.
Which bones articulate to form the knee joint?
Femur + tibia = knee; pelvis + femur = hip; tibia/fibula + talus = ankle.
Which bones form the ankle joint?
Tibia and fibula with the talus
Tibia and fibula + talus (a tarsal bone) = ankle.
The pelvis is formed by which bones?
Pelvis = ilium, ischium and pubis; it articulates with the sacrum.
Which bone type is mainly for PROTECTION, with a correct example?
Flat bones (sternum, ribs, pelvis) protect organs; long bones are mainly for movement.
Carpals and tarsals are examples of:
Short bones such as carpals and tarsals articulate with many other bones.
Which part of a long bone is compact bone and important for support?
Diaphysis (shaft) = compact bone; epiphysis (ends) = spongy bone.
What is the function of articular cartilage?
It covers bone ends to reduce friction at the joint.
In the anatomical position, the knee is ______ to the ankle.
Proximal = closer to the trunk; the knee is closer than the ankle.
The wrist is ______ to the elbow.
The sternum is ______ to the shoulders.
Medial = closer to the midline of the body.
The spine is ______ to the sternum.
Posterior = behind; the spine is behind the sternum.
A swimmer raises her arm sideways away from the body. Which movement occurs at the shoulder?
Abduction = away from the midline; adduction = towards it.
Increasing the angle at a joint
Decreasing the angle at a joint
Moving a limb away from the midline
Flexion decreases the joint angle; extension increases it.
Pointing the toes downward, as when standing on tiptoe, is called:
Plantar flexion = toes down; dorsiflexion = toes up towards the shin.
Which tissue connects bone to bone and provides joint stability?
Ligaments = bone to bone; they keep alignment and restrict abnormal movements.
Why does an overstretched ligament increase the risk of injury?
It has many blood vessels and swells
It isn't very elastic, so it may not return to its length, reducing stability
Ligaments are not very elastic; once overstretched they stay loose and the joint is less stable.
What is the main function of a tendon?
Transmit muscle force to the bone
A tendon is an extension of the muscle's fascia: when the muscle pulls, the tendon pulls the bone.
Why does a cartilage injury heal slowly?
It has too many collagen fibres
It lacks its own blood supply
Cartilage has no blood vessels or nerves (except in the perichondrium).
In cartilage, collagen fibres give ____ and elastic fibres give ____.
Collagen = strength; elastic fibres = resilience (return to shape).
The attachment of a muscle to the MOVABLE bone is the…
Insertion = moving bone; origin = fixed bone.
Which fascia layer covers EACH individual muscle fibre?
Endomysium = each fibre; perimysium = each fascicle; epimysium = whole muscle.
Which fascia layer surrounds bundles of fibres called fascicles?
Which statement about ligaments and tendons is correct?
Ligaments connect muscle to bone and are more elastic than tendons
Ligaments connect bone to bone and are thinner and less elastic than tendons
Ligaments: bone–bone, thinner, less elastic. Tendons: muscle–bone.
What do synovial joints have that fibrous and cartilaginous joints don't?
Only synovial joints have a joint cavity; they are the most mobile.
The hip is a ball-and-socket joint and the elbow a hinge joint. Which statement is correct?
The hip allows movement in more planes than the elbow
The elbow allows rotation and abduction
Both allow only flexion and extension
The hip is a fibrous joint
Ball-and-socket joints move in many directions; hinge joints only flex and extend.
The shoulder is very mobile. According to the mobility/stability relationship this means:
No link between mobility and stability
More movement = less stability = higher injury risk.

Which factors increase joint stability?
I. Bones that interlock closely
II. A large area of contact between bones
III. Overstretched ligaments
Interlocking bones and large contact area increase stability; overstretched ligaments reduce it.
The three main types of joints are:
Joints are fibrous, cartilaginous or synovial; synovial joints are then classified by movement.
The one that relaxes and lengthens
The prime mover: the muscle that contracts to produce the movement
The one connecting bone to bone
What does the ANTAGONIST do in the main (concentric) phase of a movement?
Relaxes and lengthens, working opposite the agonist
The antagonist relaxes and elongates to allow the movement.
In the lifting phase of a biceps curl (elbow flexion), which is the agonist/antagonist?
Elbow flexion: biceps contracts, triceps lengthens.
In the upward phase of a push-up the elbow extends. Which muscle is the agonist at the elbow?
Elbow extension → triceps agonist, biceps antagonist.
When kicking a ball the knee extends. What is the agonist/antagonist pair?
Knee extension: quadriceps agonist, hamstrings antagonist.
Bringing the heel to the glutes (knee flexion), the agonist is:
Knee flexion: hamstrings agonist, quadriceps antagonist.
In dorsiflexion of the ankle, the agonist/antagonist pair is:
Tibialis anterior lifts the foot; soleus lengthens.
A sprinter pushes onto the toes (plantar flexion). The agonists are:
The calf muscles plantar flex; tibialis anterior is the antagonist.
In the upward phase of a lateral raise (shoulder abduction), the agonist is:
Lifting the thigh forwards (hip flexion): agonist / antagonist?
Iliopsoas flexes the hip; gluteus maximus extends it.
During a sit-up (trunk flexion): agonist / antagonist?
Rectus abdominis flexes the trunk; erector spinae lengthens.
Which is NOT an agonist/antagonist pair from class?
Pairs act on the same joint in opposite directions; biceps and quadriceps don't share a joint.
When the agonist contracts, the antagonist relaxes
A muscle wastes away if unused
Agonist contracts → antagonist relaxes, so movement is smooth.
Slowly LOWERING a dumbbell in a curl, the biceps is under tension while lengthening. This is:
In the upward phase of a squat, the quadriceps shorten under tension. This is:
During the downward phase of a push-up, the triceps are:
Contracting eccentrically to control the lowering
They lengthen under tension to control the descent.
Holding a plank, the core muscles are under tension but do not change length. This is:
Isometric = tension with no change in length.
Which property lets muscle respond to a nerve impulse?
Which property lets a stretched muscle return to its original length without damage?
After six weeks without training, an athlete's quadriceps become smaller. This is:
Atrophy = wasting from lack of use.
Which type of muscle tissue is under voluntary control?
Skeletal = voluntary; cardiac and smooth = involuntary.
Muscles make up roughly what share of body weight?
There are over 600 muscles, about 40–50% of body weight (the skeleton is about 20%).
The diagram shows a neuron. Which letter labels the myelin sheath?
C is the myelin sheath that insulates the axon.
Structure D is a gap between sections of myelin. What is it and what does it do?
Node of Ranvier; aids transmission of the signal
D is a node of Ranvier.
A labels a dendrite, which links to other neurons.
Which letter labels the soma (cell body)?
A hand touches a flame. Neuron B carries the impulse:
From the CNS to the muscle
From the receptor to the CNS
From the brain to the spinal cord
Which letter labels the efferent (motor) neuron?
D carries the command out of the spinal cord.
Structure C links neuron B to neuron D in the spinal cord. C is:
E is the muscle that carries out the response.
The green structure A contains the thalamus and hypothalamus. It is the:
A gymnast relies on which letter for balance and coordination?
Which letter regulates breathing and heart rate and connects the brain to the spinal cord?
Region D, the outer layer of the brain, is responsible for:
Conscious thought, voluntary movement and perception
Neuron X stimulates many fibres, neuron Y few. Which is correct?
Y gives larger forces than X
Y is typical of eye muscles: small forces, great precision
Both have the same innervation ratio
Low innervation ratio (Y) = precision; high (X) = force.
P and Q in the muscle and tendon send information about the muscle to the spinal cord. They are:
Receptors in muscles, tendons and joints are proprioceptors.
In Image 1 the elbow is flexed. Which muscle is the agonist?
From Image 1 to Image 2 the elbow extends. In Image 2, identify agonist and antagonist.
An athlete lowers a dumbbell slowly from Image 1 to Image 2. Muscle A is contracting:
The biceps lengthens under tension: eccentric.
Which letter shows the layer covering the entire muscle?
Layer C surrounds each individual muscle fibre. It is the:
Structure D joins muscle to bone. Its function is to:
Transmit muscle force to the bone
Region B is the shaft of a long bone. It is the:
What is the function of C at the end of the bone?
Tissue D fills the epiphysis and has many spaces. It is:
A footballer kicks a ball (knee extension). Which letter is the agonist?
Muscle F lifts the toes towards the shin. Name F and its antagonist.
A swimmer raises her arm sideways (abduction). Which letter is the agonist?
Which letter shows the muscle that flexes the elbow in a biceps curl?
Which letter is the rectus abdominis, agonist in a sit-up?
During knee extension, which letter is the antagonist?
Pectorals/latissimus dorsi is a muscle pair. Which letter is latissimus dorsi?
Pushing onto the toes (plantar flexion), which letter is an agonist?
Which letter is the gluteus maximus, antagonist of the iliopsoas in hip flexion?
These athletes are finishing a 100 m sprint. Which motor units do they rely on most?
Type IIb: fastest, strongest, fatigue quickly.
Before the start, the sprinters' heart and breathing rates rise. This is caused by the:
These walkers are on a three-hour hike. Which motor units are mainly used?
Type I: long, low-intensity, fatigue resistant.
